title: ArcJet
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 3 of 40
content:
ArcJet Systems had been built by people who believed the future would be clean.

I could see it in the bones of the place. Smooth walls. Curved signs. Cheerful diagrams explaining rockets and fusion and the inevitable upward march of human ingenuity. Two hundred years later, the floors were littered with shell casings and synthetic limbs.

Danse studied an old promotional poster as we passed.

“Pre-War arrogance,” he said.

“Coming from the man in power armor?”

“My armor works.”

“So did the rockets, presumably.”

“They also built the technology that destroyed the world.”

I looked at the faded family smiling beneath a painted starship.

“People destroyed the world.”

“People with technology they weren’t prepared to control.”

There it was again. The belief beneath everything.

I had heard Brotherhood rhetoric before, usually from traders complaining about patrols confiscating things. From Danse it sounded less like propaganda and more like a wound that had scarred into a philosophy.

He caught me looking at him.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You were about to say something.”

“I was deciding whether it was worth arguing while surrounded by killer robots.”

“Synths.”

“Killer synths.”

“That’s more accurate.”

“I’m glad we resolved that.”

The next room contained enough of them to end the discussion.

Danse moved first. He always did.

I had begun recognizing his combat rhythm: two shots, shift position, check my location, advance. Even when he was angry, even when the synths seemed to make something inside him go cold, he kept accounting for me.

Once, when a laser burst forced me behind a broken console, he put himself directly between me and the fire.

“Danse!”

“Stay down!”

“I can shoot from down here!”

“Then do it!”

So I did.

We fought our way into a laboratory where half-built machinery hung from the ceiling like the skeletons of mechanical animals. The deep-range signal was stronger here. Haylen’s detector clipped to Danse’s belt chirped faster.

He consulted it.

“Below us.”

“Of course it is.”

“Problem?”

“Everything dangerous in the Commonwealth is either underground or on a roof.”

“That’s objectively false.”

“I appreciate your commitment to accuracy.”

He led us down.

The engine core was enormous.

The chamber opened beneath us in a cylindrical drop, all steel gantries and pipes wrapped around a central rocket assembly. Even dead, the machine felt dangerous. Warning placards covered the walls. Emergency lights blinked weakly through dust.

Danse stared down at the engine.

“Incredible.”

The word slipped out without rank or caution.

I looked at him instead of the machinery.

For the first time since Cambridge, he sounded openly impressed.

“You like this stuff.”

“This technology represents decades of engineering.”

“That means yes.”

“It means it should be preserved and understood.”

“Still yes.”

He ignored me and moved toward the control room.

The power was out. The elevator was dead. The signal source was somewhere above us, inaccessible until we restored the facility.

I found the auxiliary controls behind a locked service door.

Danse found more synths.

The two discoveries happened almost simultaneously.

“Get the power online!” he ordered.

“You sure?”

“Do it!”

Laser fire struck the railing beside him.

I ran.

The terminal was older than anything I had used in months and twice as stubborn. My fingers slipped once on the keys because I could hear Danse fighting below. Red flashes lit the control-room windows. Metal struck metal. His rifle cracked with its distinctive electric snap.

Then the emergency system came alive.

A warning filled the chamber.

ENGINE TEST SEQUENCE ARMED.

I froze.

Below me, Danse was standing directly beneath the rocket.

“Danse!”

His helmet tilted up.

The warning repeated.

“Get out of there!”

“There’s nowhere to go!”

I looked at the control panel.

There were two choices: abort and leave him with a growing wave of synths, or fire the engine and pray power armor deserved its reputation.

More synths came through the lower doors.

Danse saw them.

Then he looked up at me.

“Do it!”

My hand hovered over the ignition control.

“No.”

“Do it!”

“That will cook you!”

“My armor can take it!”

“You don’t know that!”

“I know we’re out of options!”

He fired into the advancing line.

One synth dropped. Five more replaced it.

“Now!”

I hit the button.

The world became fire.

Even behind reinforced glass, the roar punched through my chest. White-orange exhaust filled the chamber. The rocket engine screamed against two centuries of silence. Synth silhouettes vanished inside the flame.

So did Danse.

For several seconds I could see nothing.

I had killed him.

The thought arrived whole.

Not maybe.

Not if.

I had listened to him. I had followed the order. I had pressed the button.

The test ended.

Flame collapsed into smoke.

The chamber glowed red in places where metal had heated near melting. Charred synth pieces covered the floor.

In the center of it all lay a black shape.

I was already running before the elevator indicator turned green.

The doors opened too slowly.

I hit the lower level and nearly tripped over a synth torso.

“Danse!”

Nothing.

I reached the armor.

One gauntlet moved.

I stopped so hard my knees hurt.

The suit pushed itself upright with a tortured whine of servos.

Danse sat up.

Smoke rolled from his shoulders.

His helmet retracted.

His face was red with heat and sweat. He blinked at me.

“You look concerned.”

For a moment I could not speak.

Then anger arrived to rescue me from everything else.

“You unbelievable bastard.”

His eyebrows rose.

“I ordered you to activate the engine.”

“Yes, I remember the part where you told me to roast you alive.”

“The armor’s thermal protection—”

“I did not know the armor would hold.”

“I did.”

“You hoped.”

He opened his mouth.

Closed it.

I crouched in front of him, checking the seams of the suit for damage. My hands were shaking badly enough that I had to clench them once before continuing.

Danse noticed.

Of course he noticed.

His expression changed.

“I’m all right.”

“Stop saying that like it fixes anything.”

“I’m not injured.”

“That is not the same as all right.”

The words came out before I could reconsider them.

He went very still.

For several seconds, the only sound was the cooling engine ticking above us.

Then Danse looked away.

“No,” he said quietly. “I suppose it isn’t.”

I sat back on my heels.

Something had happened in that exchange. I did not know what.

Neither, apparently, did he.

He cleared his throat and forced himself to stand.

“We still need the transmitter.”

Naturally.

“Can you walk?”

“Yes.”

“Can you walk without pretending you’re invincible?”

“No guarantees.”

That surprised a laugh out of me.

Danse looked down at my face.

The almost-smile came back.

This time it survived long enough to become real.

Small. Tired. Crooked at one corner.

Then it was gone.

“Come on,” he said. “Mission isn’t over.”

I stood beside him.

“No,” I said, still looking at the scorched armor. “Apparently neither are you.”

He shook his head, but I caught that smile again as he turned away.

We found a security office off the main corridor after the first wave of synths.

Danse wanted thirty seconds to check the map.

I wanted thirty seconds to stop my hands from shaking.

Neither of us announced our actual reason.

He leaned over a ruined terminal while I stood watch at the door. Red emergency light moved across the back of his armor in slow pulses.

“Three more corridors,” he said. “Then access to the engine core.”

“Wonderful.”

“You sound unconvinced.”

“I’m deciding whether the robots with human voices are more or less disturbing than robots that beep.”

“Synths are not robots.”

The answer was immediate.

I looked back at him.

He had stopped working the terminal.

“What are they, then?”

“Institute constructs. Machines designed to imitate people.”

“That sounds like a robot with extra steps.”

“It’s more dangerous than that.”

There was conviction in his voice, not performance. Whatever the Brotherhood had taught him about synths, he believed it down to the bone.

“You ever met one that wasn’t shooting at you?” I asked.

“No reason to.”

That answer stayed with me.

Before I could push, a metallic footstep sounded in the corridor.

Danse moved faster than thought. One gauntleted arm swept me behind the wall as laser fire cut through the doorway where my head had been.

His body blocked mine completely.

“Contact!”

We returned fire from opposite sides of the frame. I caught one synth in the shoulder. Danse finished it. A second came around the corner and he drove forward, forcing it back with the sheer mass of the armor while I put a round through its exposed torso.

Then silence.

Danse scanned twice before lowering the rifle.

Only then did he seem to realize his left arm was still braced across me.

He removed it at once.

“Apologies.”

“For keeping my face attached?”

“For moving you without warning.”

I blinked.

The distinction mattered to him.

“It was a good call.”

“I should still have warned you.”

“There wasn’t exactly time.”

“No.”

He looked at the burn mark carved into the opposite wall.

His shoulders shifted inside the armor.

“Are you injured?”

“No.”

“Certain?”

“Yes.” I flexed both hands. “Still have all the important pieces.”

Danse nodded.

Then, very carefully, he said, “Good.”

Not *acceptable*. Not *mission capable*.

Good.

I turned toward the corridor before he could see how much I noticed.

“Three more corridors?”

“Three.”

“Lead on.”

He passed me, then stopped.

Without looking back, he added, “Your reaction time is improving.”

I smiled despite myself.

“Careful. That sounded almost like a sticker.”

His shoulders moved once.

This time I knew exactly what the sound inside the helmet meant.
